RESUMO


Plataformas

de

mídia

social

operam

como

infraestruturas

de

gestão

do

trabalho

criativo

cujas

lógicas

de

dataficação,

quando

colidem

com

profissões

de

alto

prestígio

e

jurisdição

protegida

por

lei,

como

a

medicina,

revelam

a

profunda

capacidade

desse

modelo

de

negócio

de

reorganizar

o

mundo

do

trabalho.

No

Brasil,

a

expansão

do

ensino

médico

gerou

um

excedente

de

profissionais

indiferenciados

em

busca

de

diferenciação.

Nesse

cenário,

as

plataformas

emergem

como

mercados

paralelos

de

credenciais.

Esta

tese

investiga

como

influenciadores

digitais

médicos

gerenciam

a

impossibilidade

estrutural

de

conciliar

o

Profissionalismo

Organizacional

de

Plataforma

(POP),

cujo

mecanismo

central

é

a

Credencial

Performativa,

e

o

Profissionalismo

Ocupacional

Médico

(MOP),

regulado

pelo

Conselho

Federal

de

Medicina

(CFM)

sob

o

imperativo

da

Proteção

da

Autoridade

Fiduciária.

O

estudo

se

fundamenta

na

ontologia

do

Realismo

Crítico

e

no

ciclo

morfogenético

(Bhaskar,

2008;

Archer,

2020),

operacionalizado

por

meio

da

Teoria

Fundamentada

Construtivista

(Charmaz,

2014),

dentro

da

lente

analítica

da

Sociologia

das

Profissões.

A

pesquisa

examinou

materiais

instrucionais

do

Instagram,

TikTok

e

YouTube,

documentos

normativos

do

CFM,

e

analisou

sistematicamente

os

rastros

digitais

naturalísticos

de

26

mega-influenciadores

médicos

(MMI)

brasileiros

com

mais

de

um

milhão

de

seguidores

em

ao

menos

uma

dessas

plataformas.

Esta

tese

demonstrou

que,

quando

uma

profissão

organizada

em

torno

da

autoridade

fiduciária

é

submetida

à

lógica

de

credenciamento

performativo

das

plataformas

de

mídia

social,

a

autoridade

profissional

não

declina

nem

se

hibridiza;

ela

se

reconfigura,

de

forma

contínua

e

performativa,

em

direções

dialeticamente

opostas

conforme

a

orientação

teleológica

do

agente.

A

teoria

substantiva

da

Reconfiguração

Performativa

da

Autoridade

Profissional

explica

que,

diante

da

impossibilidade

estrutural

de

adesão

simultânea

ao

POP

e

ao

MOP,

os

MMI

reconfiguram

continuamente

sua

autoridade

como

uma

performance

responsiva

por

meio

de

dois

vetores

teleologicamente

opostos:

o

Vetor

1

(Conversão

da

Autoridade

Profissional

em

Ativos

Comerciais)

direciona

a

ação

para

a

conversão

comercial,

e

o

Vetor

2

(Profissionalização

da

Comunicação

em

Saúde)

se

volta

para

a

preservação

institucional

da

profissão.

Ambos

os

vetores

mobilizam

transversalmente

os

mesmos

Mecanismos

Operacionais

de

Adaptação

a

Plataformas

(OMPA).

Essa

reconfiguração

não

é

um

processo

em

equilíbrio,

pois

o

Vetor

1

praticado

em

escala

erode

as

condições

institucionais

que

tornam

o

Vetor

2

possível,

produzindo

elaboração

estrutural

em

vez

de

reprodução

da

autoridade

médica.

A

dataficação

da

autoridade

médica

e

a

emergência

de

um

sistema

paralelo

de

validação

evidenciam

que

a

plataformização

reconfigura

mesmo

a

ocupação

mais

protegida

do

trabalho

especializado.

ABSTRACT


Social

media

platforms

operate

as

infrastructures

of

creative

labor

management

whose

datafication

logics,

when

they

collide

with

high-prestige

professions

operating

under

legally

protected

jurisdictions,

such

as

medicine,

reveal

the

profound

capacity

of

this

business

model

to

reorganize

the

world

of

work.

In

Brazil,

the

expansion

of

medical

education

has

generated

a

surplus

of

undifferentiated

professionals

seeking

differentiation.

In

this

context,

platforms

emerge

as

parallel

credential

markets.

This

thesis

investigates

how

medical

digital

influencers

manage

the

structural

impossibility

of

reconciling

Platform

Organizational

Professionalism

(POP),

whose

core

mechanism

is

the

Performative

Credential,

and

Medical

Occupational

Professionalism

(MOP),

regulated

by

the

Federal

Council

of

Medicine

(CFM)

under

the

imperative

of

Fiduciary

Authority

Protection.

The

study

is

grounded

in

the

Critical

Realist

ontology

and

the

morphogenetic

cycle

(Bhaskar,

2008;

Archer,

2020),

operationalized

through

Constructivist

Grounded

Theory

(Charmaz,

2014),

within

the

analytical

lens

of

the

Sociology

of

Professions.

The

research

examined

instructional

materials

from

Instagram,

TikTok,

and

YouTube,

normative

documents

from

the

CFM,

and

systematically

analyzed

the

naturalistic

digital

traces

of

26

Brazilian

medical

mega-influencers

(MMI)

with

more

than

one

million

followers

on

at

least

one

of

these

platforms.

This

thesis

demonstrated

that,

when

a

fiduciary

authority-based

profession

is

subject

to

social

media

platforms’

logic

of

performative

credentialing,

professional

authority

does

not

decline

or

hybridize;

it

reconfigures,

continuously

and

performatively,

in

dialectically

opposing

directions

depending

on

the

agent's

teleological

orientation.

The

substantive

theory

of

Performative

Reconfiguration

of

Professional

Authority

explains

that,

given

the

structural

impossibility

of

simultaneous

adherence

to

POP

and

MOP,

MMI

continuously

reconfigure

their

authority

as

a

responsive

performance

through

two

teleologically

opposed

vectors:

Vector

1

(Converting

Professional

Authority

into

Commercial

Assets)

directs

action

toward

commercial

conversion,

and

Vector

2

(Professionalizing

Health

Communication)

is

oriented

toward

the

institutional

preservation

of

the

profession.

Both

vectors

transversally

mobilize

the

same

Operational

Mechanisms

of

Platform

Adaptation

(OMPA).

This

reconfiguration

is

not

a

process

in

equilibrium,

because

Vector

1

practiced

at

scale

erodes

the

institutional

conditions

that

make

Vector

2

possible,

producing

structural

elaboration

rather

than

the

reproduction

of

medical

authority.

The

datafication

of

medical

authority

and

the

emergence

of

a

parallel

validation

system

evidence

that

platformization

reconfigures

even

the

most

protected

occupation

in

specialized

work.

DECLARATION

OF

ARTIFICIAL

INTELLIGENCE

USE


The

use

of

artificial

intelligence

(AI)

tools

in

this

doctoral

thesis

happened

in

different

research

stages.

Data

construction

involved

the

development

of

Python

scripts,

written

with

the

support

of

Gemini

and

ChatGPT,

to

capture

data

and

content

produced

by

the

investigated

medical

influencers

on

social

media

platforms,

as

described

in

subsection

5.4.3.2.

Claude

Pro

and

QuillBot

Premium

were

used

to

review

the

language

and

assess

the

coherence,

clarity,

and

cohesion

of

the

arguments

expressed

in

English.

More

specifically,

Claude

identified

expressions

that

might

lose

their

intended

meaning

or

sound

awkward

when

translated

literally

from

Portuguese.

Each

suggestion

had

to

be

evaluated

individually

to

determine

whether

the

change

was

to

be

implemented

or

a

localized

solution

was

to

be

developed.

After

this

translation

process

with

Claude,

the

text

was

grammar

checked

by

QuillBot.

This

was

an

iterative

process

and

involved

the

manual

reading

of

small

sections

of

the

thesis.

Such

revision

ensured

the

final

version

remained

faithful

to

the

original

formulations.

The

analytical

work

remained

independent

of

automated

intervention.

The

coding

of

social

media

data,

the

development

of

categories,

and

the

formulation

of

the

substantive

theory

resulted

from

manual

analysis.

This

effort

involved

co-authors

during

Phase

1

and

proceeded

individually

in

Phases

2

and

3.

Full

responsibility

for

the

content,

theoretical

interpretations,

and

intellectual

integrity

of

this

doctoral

thesis

rests

with

the

author.

within

the

economy

has

The

individuals

and

original

This

work,

economy

2019

onward

the

the

segment

toward

teaching

something,

and

onward

phenomenon

Alongside

The

The

Medicine

is

a

case

in

point,

and

if

an

occupation

with

that

institutional

this

full

of

this

business

medicine

(MacDonald,

1995;

Rodrigues,

2002;

Saks,

2016).

Functionalism

addresses

professions

in

terms

of

social

differentiation,

role

division,

and

socialization.

These

special

occupations

are

considered

ethically

positive

entities

that

embody

core

societal

values

and

incorporate

socially

functional

traits

such

as

altruism

and

are

therefore

considered

a

moral

basis

for

modern

society

(MacDonald,

1995,

p.

2).

The

functionalist

Talcott

Parsons,

whose

work

drew

on

Weberian

concepts,

was

the

first

to

demonstrate

the

relationship

between

the

capitalist

economy,

the

rational-legal

social

order,

and

modern

professions

(Rodrigues,

2002;

Evetts,

2013).

He

conceptualized

the

professional

role

through

dimensions

that

articulated

social

norms

and

cultural

values,

such

as

dual

competence

involving

both

practical

and

theoretical

knowledge

and

a

sense

of

37

disinterestedness

that

combined

affective

neutrality

with

client-oriented

service.

Parsons

argued

that,

despite

having

the

same

rational-legal

principles

as

the

managerial

hierarchy

of

bureaucratic

organizations,

professions

differ

by

seeking

a

shared

normative

end

through

collegiate

organization

(Evetts,

2013;

2018).


Although

Parsons

went

beyond

the

taxonomy

of

other

functionalists,

he

was

criticized

for

omitting

conflicts

based

on

interests

and

professional

power

as

drivers

of

change

(Saks,

2016).

Furthermore,

his

work

was

predominantly

deductive,

lacking

empirical

grounding,

and

his

conceptual

system

often

justified

the

status

of

established

professions

based

on

the

ideology

of

those

same

groups

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015).


The

interactionists’

procedure

runs

counter

to

the

functionalist

approach.

Symbolic

interactionist

Everett

Hughes,

through

empirical

research

conducted

with

his

students

at

the

Chicago

School

from

the

1940s

onward,

fundamentally

challenged

the

functionalist

model

by

questioning

its

valorative

assumptions

(Rodrigues,

2002).

Hughes

(1964,

p.

44-45)

viewed

professions

as

“not

so

much

a

descriptive

term

as

one

of

value

and

prestige,”

rejecting

the

false

question

of

whether

an

occupation

qualifies

as

a

profession.

Instead,

he

investigated

the

circumstances

under

which

occupational

groups

attempt

to

transform

themselves

into

professions.

His

research

demonstrated

that

all

occupations

(from

physicians

and

lawyers

to

janitors

and

exotic

dancers)

develop

collective

pretensions,

systems

of

mutual

protection

around

mistakes,

and

claims

to

dignify

their

work,

though

they

differ

in

their

success

in

obtaining

societal

recognition

(Hughes,

1964;

1993).

In

this

perspective,

Hughes’s

followers

analyze

professionalization

as

a

process

of

mobilizing

resources

to

ascend

the

occupational

hierarchy

by

obtaining

the

honorific

title

of

a

profession

and

achieving

what

Hughes

(1993)

describes

as

occupational

mobility.

This

processual

approach

introduced

key

analytical

concepts

such

as

‘license’

or

the

authorization

to

practice;

‘mandate,’

which

represents

the

mission

and

obligation

to

define

proper

client

conduct

(Hughes,

1993);

‘career,’

understood

both

as

an

objective

sequence

of

positions

and

a

subjective

self-interpretation

(Hughes,

1937);

and

‘guilty

knowledge,’

which

involves

handling

the

sacred

and

taboo

matters

of

society

(Hughes,

1964;

1993).

Expanding

the

procedural

framework,

Rue

Bucher

and

Anselm

Strauss

conceived

of

professions

as

flexible

professional

segments

in

constant

flux,

rather

than

homogeneous

communities

sharing

unified

identities

and

interests,

as

the

functionalists

assumed

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Rodrigues,

2002).

These

segments

are

defined

by

divergent

missions,

methodologies,

clients,

and

career

paths,

and

this

internal

diversity

leads

them

to

38

continuous

conflict

over

jurisdictional

boundaries,

resources,

and

the

legitimate

mandate

of

the

profession.

Freidson

(1996)

identified

the

structural

source

of

this

tension

as

a

division

between

a

cognitive

elite

of

academic

authority

and

practitioners

in

their

daily

work.

Because

these

groups

operate

under

different

standards,

there

is

inherent

conflict

within

the

professional

structure.

In

addition

to

reflecting

status

variations,

internal

differentiation

serves

to

generate

or

absorb

disturbances

in

interprofessional

relationships,

according

to

Abbott

(1988),

allowing

professions

to

respond

to

external

challenges

with

internal

reconfigurations

instead

of

frontal

confrontation.

From

an

interactionist

perspective,

professionalization

involves

internal

differentiation

marked

by

hierarchies

among

elite

groups

of

researchers

in

universities,

professionals,

and

administrators,

each

group

claiming

to

represent

true

professionalism

while

marginalizing

the

others

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Freidson,

1996;

Rodrigues,

2002).

While

these

interactionist

insights

remained

focused

on

workplace

negotiations

and

internal

professional

dynamics

(Saks,

2014;

2016),

subsequent

theorists,

such

as

Freidson

(2007)

and

Larson

(2017),

expanded

this

processual

logic

to

analyze

broader

public

and

legal

contexts,

shifting

the

unit

of

analysis

from

the

profession

itself

to

interprofessional

relations,

as

Abbott

(1988)

does.

The

shift

from

internal

negotiations

to

interprofessional

relations

requires

a

broader

approach

to

power.

Interactionism

anticipated

power-centered

perspectives

by

exposing

how

functionalists

reified

professional

self-representations

(Hughes,

1964).

However,

MacDonald

(1995)

and

Saks

(2016)

believe

the

interactionist

view

is

limited

by

its

micro-focus

on

workplace

negotiations

and

the

subjective

construction

of

meaning,

overlooking

larger

power

dynamics,

historical

processes,

and

how

state

recognition

affects

professional

success.

Although

interactionism’s

emphasis

on

professionalization

as

a

strategic

and

symbolic

action

has

influenced

later

theories

on

professional

power

and

social

closure,

analytical

tools

are

insufficient

to

explain

why

some

occupational

projects

secure

state-sanctioned

monopolies

while

others

fail.

Since

the

1970s,

authors

have

focused

on

this

issue,

shifting

the

emphasis

from

microsociological

to

macrostructural

analyses

of

power

and

social

closure

(Saks,

2010).

The

evolution

of

the

discipline

demonstrates

that

professions

are

projects

vulnerable

to

external

forces.

For

medical

influencers,

one

form

of

exposure

to

vulnerability

is

the

governance

logic

of

platforms,

potentially

incompatible

with

medical

professionalism.

The

next

section

explores

the

neo-Weberian

framework,

which

offers

the

analytical

vocabulary

needed

to

examine

the

tension

between

professional

projects,

autonomy,

jurisdiction,

and

knowledge.

39


3.2

Neo-Weberian

perspectives

on

closure,

monopoly,

and

control

Critical

perspectives

in

Anglo-American

sociology

of

professions

encompass

diverse

paradigmatic

and

methodological

orientations.

Although

this

heterogeneous

body

can

be

classified

as

a

power

paradigm

(Rodrigues,

2002),

this

thesis

adopts

the

neo-Weberian

designation

used

by

Dubar,

Tripier,

and

Boussard

(2015),

MacDonald

(1995),

and

Saks

(2016).

Neo-Weberian

authors

draw

on

symbolic

interactionism

and

Marxism,

yet

analytical

tools

from

Weber’s

work

remain

central,

enabling

adaptability

across

organizational

contexts

without

constituting

theoretical

inconsistency

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015).

Weber

rarely

used

the

term

“profession,”

conceiving

professionalism

as

associated

with

rational

action

in

relation

to

ends

and

values

(Schmitz,

2014,

p.

22),

which

provides

the

basis

for

understanding

professions

as

groups

that

strategically

seek

to

institutionalize

authority

through

exclusionary

strategies

(Weber,

1922/2002).

Work

as

a

vocation

(
beruf
),

which

was

once

rooted

in

the

Protestant

ethic,

is

transformed

by

economic

rationalization

that

leads

to

increasing

bureaucratization

and

the

rise

of

the

expert,

whose

legitimacy

no

longer

rests

on

charismatic

or

traditional

grounds;

professional

authority

is

now

based

on

a

belief

in

competence

attested

by

diplomas

and

loyalty

to

established

norms

(Weber,

1905/2004;

Weber,

1922/2002).

Central

to

this

approach

are

Weber’s

concepts

of

power,

as

“the

probability

that

an

actor

within

a

social

relationship

is

in

a

position

to

carry

out

his

own

will

despite

resistance”

(Weber,

2004,

p.

33).

This

is

operationalized

through

social

closure,

the

process

by

which

groups

restrict

access

to

resources

and

opportunities

for

eligible

individuals,

aiming

to

maintain

prestige,

social

honor,

and

economic

chances

(Weber,

2010).

Through

these

exclusionary

strategies,

professions

transform

de

facto

power

into

legitimate

rational-legal

authority

and,

in

this

way,

monopolize

their

advantages

in

competitive

markets

(Weber,

1922/2002).

But

monopoly

is

not

a

perpetual

status.

It

requires

the

continuous

exercise

of

linking

social

closure

to

the

practical

domain

of

labor.

Professionalism

involves

a

cognitive

dimension

where

abstract

knowledge

serves

as

a

strategic

resource

for

autonomy

and

the

control

of

jurisdictions

(Abbott,

1988;

Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Rodrigues,

2002).

Alongside

this,

a

political

dimension

exists

where

service

provision

becomes

a

point

of

negotiation

between

the

state

and

the

professions

to

maintain

practice

exclusivity

(Saks,

2010).

The

pursuit

of

legitimacy

and

market

protection

is

operationalized

through

the

professional

project

(Larson,

2017),

which

involves

the

struggle

for

control

of

jurisdictions

(Abbott,

1988)

and

the

attainment

of

autonomy

(Freidson,

2007).

40

Given

that

the

system

occupied

by

professions

and

occupations

is

strained

by

external,

relational,

and

internal

forces,

the

meanings

of

professionalism

also

change,

especially

in

the

face

of

modern

organizational

(Evetts,

2013)

and

interactional

contexts

(Goffman,

2002;

1967/1982).

This

vulnerability

becomes

particularly

visible

when

alternative

modes

of

institutionalizing

expertise

emerge,

as

the

following

sections

demonstrate

through

the

concepts

of

professional

project,

autonomy,

jurisdiction,

and

knowledge.


3.2.1

Concepts

of

profession,

professional

project,

autonomy,

and

jurisdiction

The

neo-Weberian

and

other

critical

approaches

maintain

Hughes’s

notion

that

“a

profession

is

an

occupation

that

has

achieved

a

special

standing

among

occupations”

(Hughes,

1993,

p.

465).

This

thesis

adopts

Abbott’s

(1988,

p.

318)

definition

of

professions

as

“exclusive

occupational

groups

applying

somewhat

abstract

knowledge

to

particular

cases.”

Monopoly

represents

merely

one

form

of

jurisdictional

settlement,

being

rare,

difficult

to

maintain,

and

not

universally

sought

(Abbott,

1988).

Beyond

rejecting

market

exclusivity

as

essential,

Abbott

(1988)

and

his

peers

converge

in

classifying

professions

as

a

unique

and

privileged

occupational

type.

According

to

Freidson

(1989,

p.

425),

a

profession

is

“a

kind

of

occupation

whose

members

control

recruitment,

training,

and

the

work

they

do,”

having

the

right

to

supervise

and

evaluate

its

members’

technical

activities.

This

professional

autonomy

excludes

repetitive

tasks,

applying

only

to

activities

that

require

discretionary

judgment

based

on

theoretical

knowledge.

Furthermore,

professional

authority

is

achieved

through

persuasion,

as

the

group

must

convince

society

that

its

specialized

knowledge

deserves

exclusive

control

and

that

this

monopoly

will

serve

the

public

interest,

not

purely

selfish

ends

(Freidson,

2007).

Larson

(1979;

2017)

defines

a

professional

project

as

the

conversion

of

an

occupational

group’s

limited

resources

(particularly

knowledge

and

skills)

into

social

and

economic

rewards.

She

believes

that

social

closure

mechanisms

like

accreditation

maintain

scarcity

by

restricting

supply

in

the

labor

market.

This

process

combines

accredited

cognitive

exclusivity

with

market

closure

to

ensure

prestige

within

the

social

stratification

system.

However,

the

professional

project

is

susceptible

to

threats,

requiring

the

constant

invocation

of

the

legitimizing

ideology

before

the

state

and

the

public.

Consequently,

professions

are

special

communities

of

discourse

that

possess

the

authority

to

speak

about

and

for

their

respective

fields,

constructing

their

meaning

and

maintaining

internal

unity

to

defend

their

credibility

(Larson,

2018).

Therefore,

addressing

specialized

knowledge

and

promoting

professional

ideology

on

social

media

can

be

understood

as

a

form

of

discourse

useful

for

41

maintaining

the

collective

professional

project,

though

individual

practitioners

may

instrumentalize

this

rhetoric

for

personal

ends.

Gaining

control

over

a

territory

of

work

involves

more

than

publicly

defending

one’s

arguments;

it

also

entails

disputes

over

jurisdictional

control,

in

which

professions

compete

with

one

another

to

take

on

tasks

and

solve

problems.

According

to

Abbott

(1988),

a

“jurisdiction”

represents

the

link

between

a

profession

and

its

work,

anchored

in

formal

and

informal

structure

and

social

and

cultural

dimensions.

The

social

dimension

of

the

acquired

jurisdictional

rights

may

include

a

monopoly

on

practice,

the

right

to

self-discipline,

and

control

over

professional

training,

recruitment,

and

licensing.

The

cultural

dimension

is

supported

through

three

essential

stages,

including

the

classification

of

the

problem,

known

as

diagnosis;

the

reasoning

process,

or

inference;

and

the

final

execution

of

action,

defined

as

treatment.

While

diagnosis

expands

the

knowledge

base

and

treatment

follows

instructions

derived

from

it,

inference

remains

the

most

exclusive

to

professional

tasks.

It

uses

the

diagnosis

to

generate

treatment

options

and

predict

results,

requiring

a

cognitive

structure

that

society

recognizes

as

legitimate

for

solving

the

issues

at

hand.



3.2.2

Knowledge

as

a

necessity

and

ideological

tool

for

legitimacy

Professions

became

possible

once

knowledge

emerged

as

a

sociocultural

entity

independent

of

established

social

institutions

(such

as

monarchies

and

religions)

and

when

the

market

became

a

societal

element

enabling

private

provision

of

knowledge-based

services

(Freidson,

1995).

In

this

context,

knowledge

is

essential

for

highly

specialized

work

because

it

ensures

that

tasks

and

solutions

to

complex

problems

rest

on

rational,

logical,

and

scientific

principles

and

values

(Abbott,

1988).

Thus,

knowledge

allows

professions

to

dispute

jurisdiction,

claim

autonomy,

and

secure

social

legitimation

necessary

for

realizing

the

professional

project.

As

a

synonym

for

competence,

knowledge

reinforces

belief

in

professional

rational-legal

authority.

Abbott

(1988)

contends

that

abstract

knowledge

is

the

only

one

capable

of

rationalizing

professional

work

while

justifying

it

through

cultural

values.

Although

some

occupations

obtain

licenses

or

create

ethical

codes

(real

estate

agents,

for

example),

only

professions

grounded

in

abstract

knowledge

systems

can

defend

and

expand

jurisdiction

by

claiming

new

domains

and

tasks.

Abstract

and

concrete

knowledge

form

a

continuum

with

varying

degrees,

the

former

context-independent

and

the

latter

context-dependent.

A

profession

risks

losing

credibility

at

either

extreme,

as

excessive

abstraction

may

appear

as

mere

formalism,

while

excessive

concreteness

is

often

dismissed

as

craft

(Abbott,

1988).

42

Higher

education

institutions

serve

as

the

primary

means

of

professionalization

because

they

provide

scientific

knowledge

training

and

legitimacy

through

credentials

(Carvalho;

Santiago,

2016).

Academia

is

uniquely

suited

to

professional

field

expansion,

as

exemplified

by

medicine’s

appropriation

of

alcoholism

and

mental

illness

from

the

church

and

police.

For

Larson

(2017,

p.

XXV),

the

modern

university

provides

the

structural

link

between

market

and

technical-theoretical

knowledge,

two

previously

disconnected

entities.

The

university

combines

the

production

of

knowledge

with

that

of

“the

production

of

the

producers,”

which

standardizes

expertise

so

that

it

can

be

sold

as

a

recognizable

commodity.

The

professional

group

sets

the

training’s

content

and

duration

(if

there

is

no

organized

theoretical

body,

one

will

be

constructed)

to

meet

work

needs

and

to

prove

that

their

activity

is

a

profession.

Long-term

learning

and

training

help

to

develop

professional

identity,

prevent

the

dissemination

of

knowledge

to

the

outside,

and

maintain

supply

control

(Freidson,

2007).


A

profession’s

prestige

and

power

are

determined

by

the

nature

of

its

knowledge,

its

social

evaluation,

how

it

is

applied

to

serve

clients

and

expand

jurisdiction

(Abbott,

1988),

and

how

access

to

it

is

protected

(Freidson,

1995).

But

although

necessary,

certified

knowledge

and

credentials

are

insufficient

to

typify

a

profession

(Larson,

2018);

they

are

means

and

resources,

not

attributes

(Hughes,

1993),

because

they

can

only

have

an

impact

if

clients,

the

state,

and

broader

society

believe

in

their

worth

(Abbott,

1988;

Freidson,

1989).

Therefore,

the

professional

ideology

centers

on

the

belief

that

specialized

knowledge

and

skills

require

higher

education,

specialized

training,

and

experience,

thus

justifying

trust,

autonomy,

and

monopoly.

Professional

knowledge

and

skills

lack

inherent

power;

their

generic

resource

is

persuasion,

a

complex

task

including

“rhetorical

claims

and

institutional

practices

that

ordinary

occupations

do

not

ordinarily

display”

(Freidson,

1989,

427).

Maintaining

professional

unity

and

consensus

on

its

premises,

requires

a

continuous

discourse

in

defense

of

its

ideology

(Larson,

1979).


External

forces

pose

systematic

challenges

to

this

defense.

Alternative

modes

of

institutionalizing

expertise,

the

commodification

of

knowledge

and

employment,

compete

with

according

Abbott

(1988).

Commodification

embeds

expertise

into

products,

such

standardized

forms

or

computer

systems,

and

threatens

professional

jurisdiction

by

eliminating

the

need

for

professional

mediation

and

accessible

to

Organizational

employment

poses

a

greater

threat

it

subordinates

professional

work

to

organizational

hierarchies

and

workplace

control

over

their

tasks

(Abbott,

1988).

According

to

Larson

(2017),

market

and

disrupt

the

constitutive

link

43

between

educational

credentials

and

market

position

in

the

division

of

labor.

Credentialing

loses

to

collective

mobility

and

occupational

closure;

expertise

circulates

outside

the

profession’s

monopolistic

professionals

risk

subordination

to

organizational

imperatives

and

capitalist

profit

objectives.

The

Professions

are

advanced

'service

ideal'

ideology

For

(2001),

profession

phenomenologically

as

something

that

realized

This

The

“imperial

As

health

state

This

a

work,

the

human

deep

and

Such

a

occupations

(Abbott,

The

ability

to

abstract

from

contexts

boundaries

of

prestige

within

fields

linked

to

the

purity

or

of

work.

is

whereas

This

distinction,

(1966/2001)

or

does

44

not

categories.

deal

well-defined

emergency

or

complex

The

problem

referral

chain

arrives

and

to

higher

interprofessional

status.

successive

of

life.

The

intern

prepares

body,

the

resident

opens

it,

cardiac

surgeon

works

the

heart

alone,”

Abbott

(1988,

p.

827).

derives

from

the

ability

to

isolate

knowledge.


However,

public

logic.

The

values

those

the

important

public

peer

authority,

dynamic

on

social

media,

where

the

structural

of

work

are

Social

media

is

inherently

“frontstage”

(Goffman,

2002,

78),

space

individuals

act

and

present

an

image

of

themselves

conforms

social

as

opposed

to

the

“backstage,”

the

private

space

where

they

can

be

themselves.

Medical

influencers

must

therefore

deal

with

the

tension

between

peer

recognition,

values

purified

work,

and

public

recognition,

values

direct

engagement.

Although

many

physicians

work

within

settings,

medicine

retains

the

characteristics

of

a

liberal

profession,

the

for

identifying

traits

of

occupational

professionalism.

In

contrast,

content

creation

for

is

an

from

and

logic

of

platforms.

As

established

in

Chapter

2,

the

of

creation

for

media

lacks

them

and

is

directly

subject

to

the

governance

and

interests

of

specific

organizations.


Medicine

and

relate

to

respective

differently.

(2005)

explains

that

actors

connect

tasks

through

'ligation,'

an

interaction

defines

the

the

location,

the

between

traditional

an

exclusive

and

stable

jurisdiction.

argue

performance

metrics

function

what

explains

3.3

The

turn

from

profession

to

professionalism

All

attempts

to

characterize

professions

are

ideal

types,

that

is,

heuristic

constructs

that

guide

hypothetical

approaches

to

the

historical

development

of

certain

occupations.

However,

according

to

Nunes

and

Souza

(2017),

the

common

traits

that

helped

explain

the

rise

of

traditional

professions

in

the

20th

century

are

now

insufficient

to

account

for

contemporary

transformations

driven

by

external

factors

such

as

technology

and

globalization,

as

well

as

new

forms

of

identity

driven

by

consumption.

Turning

analytical

attention

toward

professionalism

offers

a

better

path

for

understanding

these

changes.

Professionalism

highlights

the

importance

of

trust

in

economic

relations

within

modern

societies

characterized

by

advanced

divisions

of

labor.

In

everyday

language,

to

say

that

a

group

is

professional

means

that

it

prioritizes

clients,

maintains

confidentiality,

refrains

from

using

knowledge

fraudulently,

and

thereby

deserves

laypeople’s

trust

(Evetts,

2006).

Professionalism

may

thus

be

a

distinct

form

of

decentralized

occupational

control,

that

is,

self-regulation

embedded

in

each

practitioner

through

shared

norms

and

values.


Professionalism

is

theorized

through

distinct

lenses

across

the

literature.

Freidson

(2007)

posits

professionalism

as

a

third

logic

of

work

organization,

an

ideal

type

whose

normative

values,

centered

on

logic

and

integrity,

organize

work

as

an

alternative

to

rational-legal

bureaucracy

(managerialism,

where

managers

control

work)

and

the

free

labor

market

(consumerism,

where

customers’

preferences

control

work).

The

institutional

arrangement

stems

from

the

belief

that

professional

work

is

so

specialized

that

it

is

inaccessible

to

untrained

individuals

and

cannot

be

standardized

or

commodified.

Digital

platforms,

however,

are

simultaneously

market

mechanisms

and

algorithmic

standardization,

a

combination

that

Freidson’s

typology

did

not

anticipate.


Conversely,

Larson

(1979)

sees

professionalism

as

an

ideology

that

both

describes

real

social

relations

and

produces

imaginary

narratives

to

ensure

systemic

conformity.

This

46

ideology

expresses

bourgeois

individualism

built

around

the

private

appropriation

of

socially

generated

skills.

In

this

view,

the

idea

that

science

and

rational

knowledge

are

neutral

serves

to

justify

the

professional

privileges

and

authority,

which

in

turn

explains

the

inequalities

within

the

occupational

stratification

system

(Larson,

2017).

In

the

1990s,

researchers

reconsidered

the

positive

contributions

of

professionalism

to

social

systems,

marking

a

return

to

its

analysis

as

a

normative

value

(Evetts,

2006).

Julia

Evetts’s

constructivist

approach

gained

traction

by

shifting

the

focus

from

defining

a

profession

to

analyzing

how

discourses

of

professionalism

impact

occupational

change

(Nunes;

Souza,

2017).

As

the

positive

public

image

of

professionals

persists,

organizations

mobilize

employees’

desire

for

recognition

by

defining

professionalism

as

a

set

of

virtues

and

principles

that

guide

worker

conduct

with

corporate

goals.

Through

mechanisms

of

occupational

identity

and

self-control,

professionalism

becomes

simultaneously

an

individual

aspiration

and

a

powerful

governance

tool

(Aldridge;

Evetts,

2003).

Evetts

(2013)

has

drawn

attention

to

the

growing

centralization,

bureaucratization,

and

rationalization

of

professional

work

through

her

ideal

types

of

occupational

professionalism

and

organizational

professionalism,

built

on

Fournier’s

(1999)

understanding

of

professionalism

as

a

disciplinary

mechanism

for

governing

autonomous

labor.

These

ideal

types

distinguish

the

origin

of

professionalism

discourse,

how

it

translates

into

work

control

and

practitioner

autonomy,

and

the

mechanisms

through

which

it

operates

(as

synthesized

in

Table

3).

Saks

(2016)

notes

that

Evetts

used

Weberian

concepts

of

rational-legal

authority

instead

of

mainly

focusing

on

social

closure

and

also

drew

on

Durkheim’s

views

of

organic

solidarity

and

occupations

as

moral

communities

and

sources

of

identity

(Evetts,

2013).

Occupational

professionalism

is

a

discourse

constructed

from

within

the

group,

built

through

long-term

education,

training,

and

socialization

that

fosters

strong

collective

identities.

In

this

model,

professional

self-regulation

is

supported

by

codes

of

ethics

and

peer

supervision,

where

autonomy

to

control

one’s

work

implies

a

relationship

of

trust

between

practitioners,

employers,

and

clients.

Groups

skilled

at

using

discourse

to

construct

their

identity

and

bargain

with

the

state

are

often

those

that

secure

market

privileges

and,

consequently,

substantial

returns

in

terms

of

salary,

status,

and

authority

(Evetts,

2013).

In

contrast,

organizational

professionalism

is

a

discourse

of

control

used

by

managers

to

reconcile

individual

aspirations

with

corporate

goals.

Within

organizations,

those

in

higher

hierarchical

positions

set

the

standards

for

actions,

aligning

the

conduct

of

subordinates

with

business

interests

(Evetts,

2018).

This

model

is

based

on

rational-legal

authority

and

a

top-down

approach.

Instead

of

relying

on

peer

trust,

it

holds

professionals

accountable

47

through

standardized

procedures

and

performance

monitoring

(Evetts,

2013).

Corporate

objectives

regulate

and

replace

the

practitioner’s

control

in

professional-client

interactions,

limiting

discretionary

judgment

(Evetts,

2018).

Workers

welcome

the

discourse

of

professionalism

if

they

perceive

it

as

a

means

of

obtaining

rewards

or

status,

even

constrains

their

autonomy

(Aldridge;

2003).

ABSTRACT


Social

media

platforms

operate

as

infrastructures

of

creative

labor

management

whose

datafication

logics,

when

they

collide

with

high-prestige

professions

operating

under

legally

protected

jurisdictions,

such

as

medicine,

reveal

the

profound

capacity

of

this

business

model

to

reorganize

the

world

of

work.

In

Brazil,

the

expansion

of

medical

education

has

generated

a

surplus

of

undifferentiated

professionals

seeking

differentiation.

In

this

context,

platforms

emerge

as

parallel

credential

markets.

This

thesis

investigates

how

medical

digital

influencers

manage

the

structural

impossibility

of

reconciling

Platform

Organizational

Professionalism

(POP),

whose

core

mechanism

is

the

Performative

Credential,

and

Medical

Occupational

Professionalism

(MOP),

regulated

by

the

Federal

Council

of

Medicine

(CFM)

under

the

imperative

of

Fiduciary

Authority

Protection.

The

study

is

grounded

in

the

Critical

Realist

ontology

and

the

morphogenetic

cycle

(Bhaskar,

2008;

Archer,

2020),

operationalized

through

Constructivist

Grounded

Theory

(Charmaz,

2014),

within

the

analytical

lens

of

the

Sociology

of

Professions.

The

research

examined

instructional

materials

from

Instagram,

TikTok,

and

YouTube,

normative

documents

from

the

CFM,

and

systematically

analyzed

the

naturalistic

digital

traces

of

26

Brazilian

medical

mega-influencers

(MMI)

with

more

than

one

million

followers

on

at

least

one

of

these

platforms.

This

thesis

demonstrated

that,

when

a

fiduciary

authority-based

profession

is

subject

to

social

media

platforms’

logic

of

performative

credentialing,

professional

authority

does

not

decline

or

hybridize;

it

reconfigures,

continuously

and

performatively,

in

dialectically

opposing

directions

depending

on

the

agent's

teleological

orientation.

The

substantive

theory

of

Performative

Reconfiguration

of

Professional

Authority

explains

that,

given

the

structural

impossibility

of

simultaneous

adherence

to

POP

and

MOP,

MMI

continuously

reconfigure

their

authority

as

a

responsive

performance

through

two

teleologically

opposed

vectors:

Vector

1

(Converting

Professional

Authority

into

Commercial

Assets)

directs

action

toward

commercial

conversion,

and

Vector

2

(Professionalizing

Health

Communication)

is

oriented

toward

the

institutional

preservation

of

the

profession.

Both

vectors

transversally

mobilize

the

same

Operational

Mechanisms

of

Platform

Adaptation

(OMPA).

This

reconfiguration

is

not

a

process

in

equilibrium,

because

Vector

1

practiced

at

scale

erodes

the

institutional

conditions

that

make

Vector

2

possible,

producing

structural

elaboration

rather

than

the

reproduction

of

medical

authority.

The

datafication

of

medical

authority

and

the

emergence

of

a

parallel

validation

system

evidence

that

platformization

reconfigures

even

the

most

protected

occupation

in

specialized

work.

INTRODUCTION

Industries

built

on

creative

work

were

among

the

first

to

absorb

the

consequences

of

platform

logic,

but

its

reach

has

since

extended

to

professions

with

legally

protected

jurisdictions

and

consolidated

social

prestige,

reorganizing

labor

well

beyond

the

sectors

where

its

influence

was

initially

felt.

Social

media

platforms

are

organizations

that

manage

the

productive

labor

of

those

who

use

them,

even

when

that

management

operates

through

indirect

means.

Proprietary

organizations

inscribe

their

values

and

interests

into

their

platforms’

codes,

which

means

having

the

power

to

define

and

impose

rules

on

those

who

produce

within

them

(Dolara;

Schrape,

2023).

It

is

within

this

organizational

space

that

the

creator

economy

has

taken

shape.

The

creator

economy

is

structured

around

the

individuals

who

create,

distribute,

and

market

original

content

through

digital

platforms.

This

activity

generated

a

market

that

transformed

online

content

production

into

a

structured

form

of

work,

remuneration,

and

entrepreneurship

(Ma;

Gui;

Kou,

2023).

The

most

significant

change

within

this

economy

from

2019

onward

was

the

rapid

growth

of

the

segment

oriented

toward

teaching

something,

from

parenting

advice

and

history

lessons

to

parenting

guidance

(Hund;

Grohmann,

2022).

Healthcare

professionals

are

part

of

this

growing

group,

and

their

participation

intensified

from

2020

onward

with

the

COVID-19

pandemic

(Farsi,

2021),

although

the

phenomenon

of

medical

digital

influencers

had

already

been

studied

by

medical

researchers

since

the

2010s

(Alhafez;

Rubio-Rico;

Diez-Bosch,

2023).

Alongside

the

growth

of

medical

influencers,

marketing

agencies

specializing

in

this

segment

have

emerged.

The

engagement

of

individuals

from

highly

institutionalized

professions

in

digital

content

creation

corroborates

Grohmann’s

(2021)

claim

that

dependence

on

digital

platforms

to

obtain

work

or

carry

out

occupational

activities

tends

toward

generalization.

The

force

of

this

phenomenon

is

neither

anecdotal

nor

transitory.

Medicine

is

a

case

in

point,

and

if

an

occupation

with

that

institutional

standing

does

not

escape

platformization,

this

reveals

the

full

extent

of

this

business

model’s

capacity

to

capture

and

reshape

occupational

life.

Drawing

on

this

reasoning,

this

thesis

defined

medicine

as

its

empirical

domain.

Brazilian

physicians

who

are

mega-influencers,

those

with

more

than

one

million

followers

(Hawley;

Ismail,

2023),

were

chosen

as

the

empirical

focus

because

this

threshold

places

them

in

the

elite

of

the

creator

economy

in

terms

of

monetization

expectations.

At

this

scale,

the

prescriptions

of

platform

logic

are

structural

and

continuous.

A

physician

does

not

reach

that

level

of

visibility

without

sustained

alignment

with

the

behaviors

that

serve

15

platform

business

objectives

and

adherence

to

the

ethos

of

content

creation.

This

is

the

condition

that

places

the

medical

influencer

under

two

competing

normative

demands

at

once.

Medical

mega-influencers

are

at

the

top

of

a

larger

stratification

of

physicians

with

a

digital

presence;

the

structural

conditions

examined

in

this

thesis

do

not

necessarily

apply

to

physicians

in

the

early

stages

of

audience

building

or

without

consolidated

monetization.


The

physician

who

operates

as

a

mega-influencer

accumulates

two

roles

that

pull

in

different

directions.

As

a

physician,

the

individual

follows

autonomous

conduct

norms

and

exercises

discretionary

judgment,

distinct

from

professionals

subject

to

organizational

control.

These

represent

two

distinct

normative

configurations.

According

to

Evetts’

(2013)

ideal

types,

occupational

professionalism

is

a

discourse

constructed

within

the

professional

group,

based

on

shared

values

and

beliefs,

technical

and

ethical

principles

of

conduct,

and

autonomy

to

control

one’s

own

work.

Organizational

professionalism

is

a

management

control

discourse

that

defines

‘professional’

behaviors

aligned

with

corporate

objectives,

defining

standardized

procedures,

performance

monitoring,

and

hierarchical

authority.

The

medical

mega-influencer

operates

in

response

to

both,

and

their

incompatibility

is

a

contingent

condition

activated

when

a

physician

voluntarily

takes

on

both

roles.

This

thesis

therefore

poses

the

following

question:

how

do

physicians

who

simultaneously

operate

as

mega-influencers

manage

the

tensions

between

the

visibility

imperatives

of

platforms

and

the

conduct

norms

of

a

highly

institutionalized

and

legally

protected

profession?

The

general

objective

is

to

investigate

how

the

imperatives

of

social

media

platforms

bear

upon

medical

professional

practice,

analyzing

how

physicians

who

simultaneously

operate

as

mega-influencers

manage

the

demands

of

platform

visibility

and

the

norms

of

medicine’s

institutional

authority.

answer

this

guiding

pursued

four

to

the

and

Instagram,

and

the

CFM

(4)

medicine’s

institutional

responsive

of

structural

between

3.1

Functionalism

and

symbolic

interactionism

in

early

frameworks


The

social

sciences

have

long

attributed

special

significance

to

professions,

as

studying

how

they

reflect

and

shape

aspects

of

society,

such

as

the

division

of

labor,

authority,

identity,

and

ethics,

is

fundamental

to

the

interpretation

of

social

dynamics

and

interactions

between

individuals

and

institutions

(Kurtz,

2022).

For

Émile

Durkheim

and

Max

Weber,

occupations

and

professions

were

important

phenomena

to

comprehend

modern

society’s

structures

(MacDonald,

1995;

Rodrigues,

2002;

Kurtz,

2022).

While

Durkheim

viewed

occupational

groups

as

a

link

between

individuals

and

society,

Weber

focused

on

the

influence

of

work

ethic

on

contemporary

capitalism

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Schmitz,

2014).

Functionalism

initially

predominated

in

the

discipline

(until

the

end

of

the

1960s)

and

coexisted

with

the

symbolic

interactionism

of

the

Chicago

School,

followed

(in

the

1970s)

by

a

critical

movement

opposing

the

functionalist

view

(MacDonald,

1995;

Rodrigues,

2002;

Saks,

2016).

Functionalism

addresses

professions

in

terms

of

social

differentiation,

role

division,

and

socialization.

These

special

occupations

are

considered

ethically

positive

entities

that

embody

core

societal

values

and

incorporate

socially

functional

traits

such

as

altruism

and

are

therefore

considered

a

moral

basis

for

modern

society

(MacDonald,

1995,

p.

2).

The

functionalist

Talcott

Parsons,

whose

work

drew

on

Weberian

concepts,

was

the

first

to

demonstrate

the

relationship

between

the

capitalist

economy,

the

rational-legal

social

order,

and

modern

professions

(Rodrigues,

2002;

Evetts,

2013).

He

conceptualized

the

professional

role

through

dimensions

that

articulated

social

norms

and

cultural

values,

such

as

dual

competence

involving

both

practical

and

theoretical

knowledge

and

a

sense

of

37

disinterestedness

that

combined

affective

neutrality

with

client-oriented

service.

Parsons

argued

that,

despite

having

the

same

rational-legal

principles

as

the

managerial

hierarchy

of

bureaucratic

organizations,

professions

differ

by

seeking

a

shared

normative

end

through

collegiate

organization

(Evetts,

2013;

2018).


Although

Parsons

went

beyond

the

taxonomy

of

other

functionalists,

he

was

criticized

for

omitting

conflicts

based

on

interests

and

professional

power

as

drivers

of

change

(Saks,

2016).

Furthermore,

his

work

was

predominantly

deductive,

lacking

empirical

grounding,

and

his

conceptual

system

often

justified

the

status

of

established

professions

based

on

the

ideology

of

those

same

groups

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015).


The

interactionists’

procedure

runs

counter

to

the

functionalist

approach.

Symbolic

interactionist

Everett

Hughes,

through

empirical

research

conducted

with

his

students

at

the

Chicago

School

from

the

1940s

onward,

fundamentally

challenged

the

functionalist

model

by

questioning

its

valorative

assumptions

(Rodrigues,

2002).

Hughes

(1964,

p.

44-45)

viewed

professions

as

“not

so

much

a

descriptive

term

as

one

of

value

and

prestige,”

rejecting

the

false

question

of

whether

an

occupation

qualifies

as

a

profession.

Instead,

he

investigated

the

circumstances

under

which

occupational

groups

attempt

to

transform

themselves

into

professions.

His

research

demonstrated

that

all

occupations

(from

physicians

and

lawyers

to

janitors

and

exotic

dancers)

develop

collective

pretensions,

systems

of

mutual

protection

around

mistakes,

and

claims

to

dignify

their

work,

though

they

differ

in

their

success

in

obtaining

societal

recognition

(Hughes,

1964;

1993).

In

this

perspective,

Hughes’s

followers

analyze

professionalization

as

a

process

of

mobilizing

resources

to

ascend

the

occupational

hierarchy

by

obtaining

the

honorific

title

of

a

profession

and

achieving

what

Hughes

(1993)

describes

as

occupational

mobility.

This

processual

approach

introduced

key

analytical

concepts

such

as

‘license’

or

the

authorization

to

practice;

‘mandate,’

which

represents

the

mission

and

obligation

to

define

proper

client

conduct

(Hughes,

1993);

‘career,’

understood

both

as

an

objective

sequence

of

positions

and

a

subjective

self-interpretation

(Hughes,

1937);

and

‘guilty

knowledge,’

which

involves

handling

the

sacred

and

taboo

matters

of

society

(Hughes,

1964;

1993).

Expanding

the

procedural

framework,

Rue

Bucher

and

Anselm

Strauss

conceived

of

professions

as

flexible

professional

segments

in

constant

flux,

rather

than

homogeneous

communities

sharing

unified

identities

and

interests,

as

the

functionalists

assumed

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Rodrigues,

2002).

These

segments

are

defined

by

divergent

missions,

methodologies,

clients,

and

career

paths,

and

this

internal

diversity

leads

them

to

38

continuous

conflict

over

jurisdictional

boundaries,

resources,

and

the

legitimate

mandate

of

the

profession.

Freidson

(1996)

identified

the

structural

source

of

this

tension

as

a

division

between

a

cognitive

elite

of

academic

authority

and

practitioners

in

their

daily

work.

Because

these

groups

operate

under

different

standards,

there

is

inherent

conflict

within

the

professional

structure.

In

addition

to

reflecting

status

variations,

internal

differentiation

serves

to

generate

or

absorb

disturbances

in

interprofessional

relationships,

according

to

Abbott

(1988),

allowing

professions

to

respond

to

external

challenges

with

internal

reconfigurations

instead

of

frontal

confrontation.

From

an

interactionist

perspective,

professionalization

involves

internal

differentiation

marked

by

hierarchies

among

elite

groups

of

researchers

in

universities,

professionals,

and

administrators,

the

others

(Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015;

Freidson,

1996;

Rodrigues,

2002).

While

these

insights

remained

focused

on

workplace

negotiations

and

internal

professional

dynamics

(Saks,

2014;

2016),

subsequent

theorists,

such

as

Freidson

(2007)

and

Larson

(2017),

expanded

this

processual

logic

to

analyze

broader

public

and

legal

contexts,

shifting

the

unit

of

analysis

from

the

profession

itself

to

interprofessional

relations,

as

Abbott

(1988)

does.

The

shift

from

internal

negotiations

to

interprofessional

relations

requires

a

broader

approach

to

power.

Interactionism

anticipated

power-centered

perspectives

by

exposing

how

functionalists

reified

professional

self-representations

(Hughes,

1964).

However,

MacDonald

(1995)

and

Saks

(2016)

believe

the

interactionist

view

is

limited

by

its

micro-focus

on

workplace

negotiations

and

the

subjective

construction

of

meaning,

larger

power

dynamics,

historical

processes,

how

state

Although

interactionism’s

on

professionalization

as

a

strategic

and

action

influenced

later

theories

on

professional

power

and

social

closure,

analytical

are

insufficient

Since

macrostructural

analyses

of

power

and

social

(Saks,

The

the

discipline

demonstrates

that

professions

are

projects

vulnerable

to

external

For

platforms,

The

the

neo-Weberian

framework,

examine

the

tension

between

projects,

autonomy,

jurisdiction,

and

knowledge.

monopoly

on

practice,

the

right

to

self-discipline,

and

control

over

professional

training,

recruitment,

and

licensing.

The

cultural

dimension

is

supported

through

three

essential

stages,

including

the

classification

of

the

problem,

known

as

diagnosis;

the

reasoning

process,

or

inference;

and

the

final

execution

of

action,

defined

as

treatment.

While

diagnosis

expands

the

knowledge

base

and

treatment

follows

instructions

derived

from

it,

inference

remains

the

most

exclusive

to

professional

tasks.

It

uses

the

diagnosis

to

generate

treatment

options

and

predict

results,

requiring

a

cognitive

structure

that

society

recognizes

as

legitimate

for

solving

the

issues

at

hand.



3.2.2

Knowledge

as

a

necessity

and

ideological

tool

for

legitimacy

Professions

became

possible

once

knowledge

emerged

as

a

sociocultural

entity

independent

of

established

social

institutions

(such

as

monarchies

and

religions)

and

when

the

market

became

a

societal

element

enabling

private

provision

of

knowledge-based

services

(Freidson,

1995).

In

this

context,

knowledge

is

essential

for

highly

specialized

work

because

it

ensures

that

tasks

and

solutions

to

complex

problems

rest

on

rational,

logical,

and

scientific

principles

and

values

(Abbott,

1988).

Thus,

knowledge

allows

professions

to

dispute

jurisdiction,

claim

autonomy,

and

secure

social

legitimation

necessary

for

realizing

the

professional

project.

As

a

synonym

for

competence,

knowledge

reinforces

belief

in

professional

rational-legal

authority.

Abbott

(1988)

contends

that

abstract

knowledge

is

the

only

one

capable

of

rationalizing

professional

work

while

justifying

it

through

cultural

values.

Although

some

occupations

obtain

licenses

or

create

ethical

codes

(real

estate

agents,

for

example),

only

professions

grounded

in

abstract

knowledge

systems

can

defend

and

expand

jurisdiction

by

claiming

new

domains

and

tasks.

Abstract

and

concrete

knowledge

form

a

continuum

with

varying

degrees,

the

former

context-independent

and

the

latter

context-dependent.

A

profession

risks

losing

credibility

at

either

extreme,

as

excessive

abstraction

may

appear

as

mere

formalism,

while

excessive

concreteness

is

often

dismissed

as

craft

(Abbott,

1988).

42

Higher

education

institutions

serve

as

the

primary

means

of

professionalization

because

they

provide

scientific

knowledge

training

and

legitimacy

through

credentials

(Carvalho;

Santiago,

2016).

Academia

is

uniquely

suited

to

professional

field

expansion,

as

exemplified

by

medicine’s

appropriation

of

alcoholism

and

mental

illness

from

the

church

and

police.

For

Larson

(2017,

p.

XXV),

the

modern

university

provides

the

structural

link

between

market

and

technical-theoretical

knowledge,

two

previously

disconnected

entities.

The

university

combines

the

production

of

knowledge

with

that

of

“the

production

of

the

producers,”

which

standardizes

expertise

so

that

it

can

be

sold

as

a

recognizable

commodity.

The

professional

group

sets

the

training’s

content

and

duration

(if

there

is

no

organized

theoretical

body,

one

will

be

constructed)

to

meet

work

needs

and

to

prove

that

their

activity

is

a

profession.

Long-term

learning

and

training

help

to

develop

professional

identity,

prevent

the

dissemination

of

knowledge

to

the

outside,

and

maintain

supply

control

(Freidson,

2007).


A

profession’s

prestige

and

power

are

determined

by

the

nature

of

its

knowledge,

its

social

evaluation,

how

it

is

applied

to

serve

clients

and

expand

jurisdiction

(Abbott,

1988),

and

how

access

to

it

is

protected

(Freidson,

1995).

But

although

necessary,

certified

knowledge

and

credentials

are

insufficient

to

typify

a

profession

(Larson,

2018);

they

are

means

and

resources,

not

attributes

(Hughes,

1993),

because

they

can

only

have

an

impact

if

clients,

the

state,

and

broader

society

believe

in

their

worth

(Abbott,

1988;

Freidson,

1989).

Therefore,

the

professional

ideology

centers

on

the

belief

that

specialized

knowledge

and

skills

require

higher

education,

specialized

training,

and

experience,

thus

justifying

trust,

autonomy,

and

monopoly.

Professional

knowledge

and

skills

lack

inherent

power;

their

generic

resource

is

persuasion,

a

complex

task

including

“rhetorical

claims

and

institutional

practices

that

ordinary

occupations

do

not

ordinarily

display”

(Freidson,

1989,

p.

427).

Maintaining

professional

unity

and

consensus

on

its

premises,

therefore,

requires

a

continuous

discourse

in

defense

of

its

ideology

(Larson,

1979).


External

forces

pose

systematic

challenges

to

this

defense.

Alternative

modes

of

institutionalizing

expertise,

such

as

the

commodification

of

knowledge

and

organizational

employment,

compete

with

professionalism,

according

to

Abbott

(1988).

Commodification

embeds

expertise

into

products,

such

as

standardized

forms

or

computer

systems,

and

threatens

professional

jurisdiction

by

eliminating

the

need

for

professional

mediation

and

making

knowledge

accessible

to

non-specialists.

Organizational

employment

poses

a

greater

threat

since

it

subordinates

professional

work

to

organizational

hierarchies

and

routines,

reducing

professions’

workplace

control

over

their

tasks

(Abbott,

1988).

According

to

Larson

(2017),

market

rationality

and

organizational

bureaucracy

disrupt

the

constitutive

link

43

between

educational

credentials

and

market

position

in

the

division

of

labor.

Credentialing

loses

its

capacity

to

secure

collective

mobility

and

occupational

closure;

expertise

circulates

outside

the

profession’s

monopolistic

control,

and

professionals

risk

subordination

to

organizational

imperatives

and

capitalist

profit

objectives.


3.2.3

Defining

professional

and

occupational

boundaries

The

seminal

works

cited

above

provide

sufficient

descriptions

to

establish

dividing

principles

between

professions

and

other

occupations,

even

if

this

distinction

has

supposedly

been

overcome

(Evetts,

2013).

Professions

are

service-based

occupations

requiring

advanced

education,

training,

and

experience,

though

this

specification

becomes

unnecessary

as

the

discipline

shifts

focus

toward

professionalism,

a

transition

detailed

in

the

next

section.

Crucially,

this

expertise

claims

legitimacy

through

a

'service

ideal'

or

ideology

where

the

professional

is

expected

to

prioritize

the

client’s

welfare

and

public

good

over

economic

self-interest

(Freidson,

1996;

Larson,

2018).

For

Freidson

(2001),

who

also

had

approached

profession

phenomenologically

as

something

that

is

realized

or

achieved

by

different

social

actors,

researchers

must

specify

how

this

concept

is

applied.


This

thesis

emphasizes

the

capacity

of

social

media

platforms

to

affect

fully

constituted

professions

that

possess

high

levels

of

field

control

and

organized

autonomy.

The

selection

process

for

this

thesis

moved

from

classic

professions

through

“imperial

professions,”

namely,

engineering,

law,

and

medicine

(Coelho,

1999),

to

the

operational

choice

of

medicine.

As

health

is

a

universal

need,

the

medical

market

is

potentially

unlimited,

while

the

state

provides

social

closure

through

licensing

and

registration

(Larson,

2017;

Saks,

2016).

This

monopoly

relies

on

linking

a

specific

object

of

work,

the

human

body,

with

deep

and

formally

rich

knowledge.

Such

a

cognitive

abstraction

ensures

exclusive

control

over

diagnosis

and

treatment

against

rival

occupations

(Abbott,

1988;

Dubar;

Tripier;

Boussard,

2015).


The

ability

to

abstract

knowledge

from

concrete

contexts

defends

professional

jurisdictional

boundaries

while

simultaneously

building

hierarchies

of

prestige

within

professional

fields

linked

to

the

purity

or

impurity

of

the

work.

“Purity”

is

characterized

as

abstract

labor

that

was

previously

being

mediated

by

lower-status

professionals,

whereas

“impurity”

is

found

in

frontline

work

that

comes

into

direct

contact

with

social

disorder

or

organizational

and

commercial

logics.

This

distinction,

formulated

by

Abbott

(1981),

is

based

on

Douglas’s

(1966/2001)

argument

that

anything

that

crosses

categorical

boundaries

or

does

44

not

fit

into

any

category

is

considered

impure

or

dangerous.

Impurity,

then,

is

a

violation

of

cultural

categories.

Specialists

deal

with

previously

refined,

technically

well-defined

problems,

while

emergency

physicians

or

general

practitioners

deal

with

complex

and

ambiguous

human

situations.

The

problem

is

purified

in

the

referral

chain

and

arrives

refined

and

delimited

to

professionals

with

higher

interprofessional

status.

“Such

successive

purification

is,

in

fact,

the

norm

of

professional

life.

The

intern

prepares

the

body,

the

resident

opens

it,

the

cardiac

surgeon

works

with

the

heart

alone,”

exemplifies

Abbott

(1988,

p.

827).

Prestige,

then,

derives

from

the

ability

to

isolate

knowledge.


However,

public

reverence

operates

according

to

an

inverted

logic.

The

population

values

precisely

those

professionals

in

direct

contact

with

disorder,

who

are

frontline

practitioners

whom

the

profession

itself

considers

impure

and

of

lower

status

(Abbott,

1981).

This

paradox

becomes

especially

important

in

digital

settings,

because

public

involvement,

not

peer

recognition,

determines

visibility

and

authority,

a

dynamic

that

shapes

medical

communication

on

social

media,

where

the

structural

conditions

of

frontline

work

are

unavoidable.

Social

media

is

inherently

“frontstage”

(Goffman,

2002,

p.

78),

a

public

space

where

individuals

act

and

present

an

image

of

themselves

that

conforms

to

social

expectations,

as

opposed

to

the

“backstage,”

the

private

space

where

they

can

be

themselves.

Medical

influencers

must

therefore

deal

with

the

tension

between

peer

recognition,

which

values

purified

work,

and

public

recognition,

which

values

direct

engagement.

Although

many

physicians

work

within

organizational

settings,

medicine

retains

the

characteristics

of

a

liberal

profession,

making

it

the

main

field

for

identifying

traits

of

occupational

professionalism.

In

contrast,

content

creation

for

social

media

is

an

emergent

occupation

born

from

and

shaped

by

the

logic

of

social

media

platforms.

As

established

in

Chapter

2,

the

conversion

of

leisure

into

labor

within

these

systems

is

conditioned

by

the

platforms’

own

definitions

of

professionalism.

While

medicine

retains

institutional

foundations,

content

creation

for

social

media

lacks

them

and

is

directly

subject

to

the

governance

and

business

interests

of

specific

organizations.


Medicine

and

content

creation

relate

to

their

respective

work

domains

differently.

Abbott

(2005)

explains

that

actors

connect

to

tasks

through

'ligation,'

an

interaction

process

that

simultaneously

defines

the

actor,

the

location,

and

the

relationship

between

them.

In

traditional

medicine,

this

connection

occurs

through

permanent

credentials,

producing

an

exclusive

and

stable

jurisdiction.

I

argue

that

continuous

performance

metrics

function

as

ligation

for

content

creators,

they

do

not

produce

stable

jurisdictions

but

rather

what

Abbott

45

(2005)

calls

settlements,

locations

without

rigid

or

exclusive

task

boundaries

where

positions

remain

fluid

and

require

constant

renegotiation.

This

structural

distinction

between

jurisdiction

and

settlement

explains

why

medicine

qualifies

as

a

profession

while

content

creation

does

not

and

why

the

analytical

focus

must

shift

from

a

profession

as

a

structural

category

to

professionalism

a

normative

When

professions

operate

within

organizational

logics,

whether

in

hospitals

or

on

platforms,

the

analysis

must

move

toward

examining

the

origin

and

operation

of

the

norms

that

govern

each

field,

as

theorized

by

Evetts

(2013;

2018)

and

others.


3.3

The

turn

from

profession

to

professionalism

All

attempts

to

characterize

professions

are

ideal

types,

that

is,

heuristic

constructs

that

guide

hypothetical

approaches

to

the

historical

development

of

certain

occupations.

However,

according

to

Nunes

and

Souza

(2017),

the

common

traits

that

helped

explain

the

rise

of

traditional

professions

in

the

20th

century

are

now

insufficient

to

account

for

contemporary

transformations

driven

by

external

factors

such

as

technology

and

globalization,

as

well

as

new

forms

of

identity

driven

by

consumption.

Turning

analytical

attention

toward

professionalism

offers

a

better

path

for

understanding

these

changes.

Professionalism

highlights

the

importance

of

trust

in

economic

relations

within

modern

societies

characterized

by

advanced

divisions

of

labor.

In

everyday

language,

to

say

that

a

group

is

professional

means

that

it

prioritizes

clients,

maintains

confidentiality,

refrains

from

using

knowledge

fraudulently,

and

thereby

deserves

laypeople’s

trust

(Evetts,

2006).

Professionalism

may

thus

be

a

distinct

form

of

decentralized

occupational

control,

that

is,

self-regulation

embedded

in

each

practitioner

through

shared

norms

and

values.


Professionalism

is

theorized

through

distinct

lenses

across

the

literature.

Freidson

(2007)

posits

professionalism

as

a

third

logic

of

work

organization,

an

ideal

type

whose

normative

values,

centered

on

logic

and

integrity,

organize

work

as

an

alternative

to

rational-legal

bureaucracy

(managerialism,

where

managers

control

work)

and

the

free

labor

market

(consumerism,

where

customers’

preferences

control

work).

The

institutional

arrangement

stems

from

the

belief

that

professional

work

is

so

specialized

that

it

is

inaccessible

to

untrained

individuals

and

cannot

be

standardized

or

commodified.

Digital

platforms,

however,

are

simultaneously

market

mechanisms

and

algorithmic

standardization,

a

combination

that

Freidson’s

typology

did

not

anticipate.


Conversely,

Larson

(1979)

sees

professionalism

as

an

ideology

that

both

describes

real

social

relations

and

produces

imaginary

narratives

to

ensure

systemic

conformity.

This

46

ideology

expresses

bourgeois

individualism

built

around

the

private

appropriation

of

socially

generated

skills.

In

this

view,

the

idea

that

science

and

rational

knowledge

are

neutral

serves

to

justify

the

professional

privileges

and

authority,

which

in

turn

explains

the

inequalities

within

the

occupational

stratification

system

(Larson,

2017).

In

the

1990s,

researchers

reconsidered

the

positive

contributions

of

professionalism

to

social

systems,

marking

a

return

to

its

analysis

as

a

normative

value

(Evetts,

2006).

Julia

Evetts’s

constructivist

approach

gained

traction

by

shifting

the

focus

from

defining

a

profession

to

analyzing

how

discourses

of

professionalism

impact

occupational

change

(Nunes;

Souza,

2017).

As

the

positive

public

image

of

professionals

persists,

organizations

mobilize

employees’

desire

for

recognition

by

defining

professionalism

as

a

set

of

virtues

and

principles

that

guide

worker

conduct

with

corporate

goals.

Through

mechanisms

of

occupational

identity

and

self-control,

professionalism

becomes

simultaneously

an

individual

aspiration

and

a

powerful

governance

tool

(Aldridge;

Evetts,

2003).

Evetts

(2013)

has

drawn

attention

to

the

growing

centralization,

and

of

work

types

Fournier’s

(1999)

of

professionalism

disciplinary

mechanism

for

governing

autonomous

labor.

types

distinguish

the

origin

of

professionalism

discourse,

how

it

translates

into

work

control

and

practitioner

autonomy,

and

the

mechanisms

through

it

operates

(as

3).

(2016)

notes

Evetts

used

Weberian

concepts

rational-legal

authority

mainly

on

social

closure

drew

on

Durkheim’s

views

of

organic

solidarity

and

occupations

as

moral

communities

and

sources

of

identity

(Evetts,

2013).

is

a

discourse

group,

strong

codes

autonomy

to

control

one’s

work

relationship

skilled

at

those

discourse

of

Within

actions,

conduct

rational-legal

Instead

of

relying

on

peer

accountable

through
